newsitem.title: USA: Ethics complaints brought against two in House.
newsitem.headline: Ethics complaints brought against two in House.

text.p: A congressional watchdog group asked the House ethics committee Friday to investigate possible improper conduct by two senior House Republicans.

The Congressional Accountability Project brought the complaints against House Majority Whip Tom DeLay of Texas and Representative Bud Shuster of Pennsylvania, chairman of the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
It said DeLay appeared to have violated bars against linking campaign contributions to official actions and engaged in influence peddling.
The group cited apparent assistance DeLay gave to his brother Randy, a foreign lobbyist, in several areas.

In one case, it said, Representative DeLay had encouraged other members to sign a letter to administration officials urging them to intercede on behalf of the Mexican cement firm Cemex which was his brother's client.

"The vigorous assistance by Representative DeLay in support of his lobbyist brother produces the clear impression that Representative DeLay has provided special and inappropriate political favours to his brother and to Cemex," the complaint said.

Asking for an investigation into possible violations of criminal law and House rules by Shuster, the group cited his ties with his former chief of staff, transportation lobbyist Ann Eppard, and interventions with federal agencies on behalf of a business partner of his sons.

"We believe the ethics committee must respond to the enormous public appearance problem arising from the tangled web of legislative, political, financial and personal ties between Representative Shuster and lobbyist Ann Eppard," the group said.
"This unseemly relationship ... has become a serious threat to the integrity of the legislative process."
The group wrote last February to Attorney General Janet Reno asking for a Justice Department investigation into the ties between Shuster and Eppard.
In a statement, DeLay's communications director John Feehery charged that the ethics committee was being abused for political purposes by a "front group for Ralph Nader."
"This complaint (against DeLay) is so weak that the sponsor could not even get a Democrat member of Congress to file it," Feehery said.
Shuster's office had no immediate response.
